stations.title: Superior vena cava
stations.text: Deoxygenated blood from the head, neck and arms returns through the superior vena cava. It is a low-pressure vessel: 5-10 mmHg.

stations.title: Right atrium
stations.text: The right atrium collects the returning blood. The sinoatrial node, the heart's natural pacemaker, sits in its wall and fires about 60-100 times a minute.

stations.title: Right ventricle
stations.text: Through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. Contraction here pushes blood into the lungs - the pulmonary circuit, the only place where arteries carry deoxygenated blood.

stations.title: Pulmonary trunk
stations.text: The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle and splits into the left and right pulmonary arteries, one for each lung.

stations.title: Right pulmonary artery
stations.text: Inside the lungs the arteries break down into smaller and smaller branches, ending in capillaries around the alveoli. Here CO2 leaves the blood and O2 enters.

stations.title: Pulmonary veins
stations.text: Oxygenated blood comes back through four pulmonary veins - the only veins that carry oxygen-rich blood - into the left atrium.

stations.title: Left atrium
stations.text: The left atrium is the receiving chamber for the systemic circuit.

stations.title: Left ventricle
stations.text: Through the mitral valve into the left ventricle. Its wall is the thickest in the heart (8-12 mm) because it has to pump blood to the whole body.

stations.title: Ascending aorta
stations.text: Blood leaves through the aortic valve into the ascending aorta. The coronary arteries branch off immediately - the heart feeds itself first.

stations.title: Arch of the aorta
stations.text: The arch turns backwards and gives off the brachiocephalic, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, which supply the head and arms.

stations.title: Descending thoracic aorta
stations.text: The descending aorta runs down the back of the chest, giving off intercostal and oesophageal branches.

stations.title: Abdominal aorta
stations.text: Below the diaphragm it becomes the abdominal aorta: coeliac trunk, mesenteric, renal and gonadal arteries branch off here.

stations.title: Right common iliac artery
stations.text: At about the level of the navel the aorta bifurcates into the two common iliac arteries.

stations.title: Right external iliac artery
stations.text: The external iliac artery crosses under the inguinal ligament and becomes the femoral artery.

stations.title: Right femoral artery
stations.text: The femoral artery is the main supply of the leg - and a favourite site for a pulse check and for catheter access.

stations.title: Right popliteal artery
stations.text: Behind the knee the femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery, which splits into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.

stations.title: Right anterior tibial artery
stations.text: Down the front of the shin, becoming the dorsalis pedis artery on the top of the foot.

stations.title: Right dorsalis pedis artery
stations.text: Roughly 5 litres a minute leave the heart; every one of them eventually squeezes through capillaries narrower than a red blood cell is wide (about 7 um).

stations.title: Right external iliac vein
stations.text: Now the return trip. The venous tree of the limb is not segmented in BodyParts3D, so we rejoin it at the external iliac vein, where blood climbs back towards the heart.

stations.title: Right common iliac vein
stations.text: Venous blood flows upward against gravity, helped by valves and by the calf muscle pump.

stations.title: Inferior vena cava
stations.text: The inferior vena cava collects everything below the diaphragm - the largest vein in the body.

stations.title: Inferior vena cava
stations.text: It passes through the diaphragm and empties into the right atrium. The circuit closes: back where we started in about a minute.
